description: The cramfs filesystem type is a compressed read-only Linux filesystem embedded in small footprint systems. A cramfs image can be used without having to first decompress the image. Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.
title: 1.1.1.1 Ensure cramfs kernel module is not available (Automated)

description: The freevxfs filesystem type is a free version of the Veritas type filesystem. This is the primary filesystem type for HP-UX operating systems. Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.
title: 1.1.1.2 Ensure freevxfs kernel module is not available

description: The hfs filesystem type is a hierarchical filesystem that allows you to mount Mac OS filesystems. Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.
title: 1.1.1.3 Ensure hfs kernel module is not available (Automated)

description: The hfsplus filesystem type is a hierarchical filesystem designed to replace hfs that allows you to mount Mac OS filesystems. Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.
title: 1.1.1.4 Ensure hfsplus kernel module is not available (Automated)

description: The jffs2 (journaling flash filesystem 2) filesystem type is a log-structured filesystem used in flash memory devices. Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.
title: 1.1.1.5 Ensure jffs2 kernel module is not available (Automated)

description: Verify the udf kernel module is not available on the system or has been disabled.
title: 1.1.1.8 Ensure udf kernel module is not available (Automated)

description: The IEEE 1394 (FireWire) is a serial bus standard for high-speed real-time communication. Disabling FireWire protects the system against exploitation of any flaws in its implementation. Verify the firewire-core kernel module is not available on the system or has been disabled.
title: 1.1.1.9 Ensure firewire-core kernel module is not available

description: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices. This ensures that users cannot create a block or character special devices in /tmp, which is not intended to support devices.
title: 1.1.2.1.2 Ensure nodev option set on /tmp partition (Automated)

description: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. This is important for the /tmp filesystem, which is intended for temporary file storage, to prevent users from creating setuid files in /tmp.
title: 1.1.2.1.3 Ensure nosuid option set on /tmp partition (Automated)

description: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. This is important for the /tmp filesystem, which is intended for temporary file storage, to prevent users from running executable binaries from /tmp.
title: 1.1.2.1.4 Ensure noexec option set on /tmp partition (Automated)

description: The /dev/shm directory is a world-writable directory that can function as shared memory that facilitates inter process communication (IPC). Making /dev/shm its own file system allows an administrator to set additional mount options such as the noexec option on the mount, making /dev/shm useless for an attacker to install executable code.
title: 1.1.2.2.1 Ensure /dev/shm is tmpfs or a separate partition

description: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices. This ensures that users cannot attempt to create special devices in /dev/shm partitions.
title: 1.1.2.2.2 Ensure nodev option set on /dev/shm partition

description: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. Setting this option on a file system prevents users from introducing privileged programs onto the system and allowing non-root users to execute them.
title: 1.1.2.2.3 Ensure nosuid option set on /dev/shm partition

description: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. This option prevents users from executing programs from shared memory, deterring the introduction of potentially malicious software.
title: 1.1.2.2.4 Ensure noexec option set on /dev/shm partition

description: The /home directory is used to support disk storage needs of local users. Configuring /home as its own file system allows an administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev, limiting an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system.
title: 1.1.2.3.1 Ensure separate partition exists for /home (Automated)

description: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices. This ensures that users cannot create a block or character special devices in /home.
title: 1.1.2.3.2 Ensure nodev option set on /home partition (Automated)

description: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. This is important for the /home filesystem, which is intended for user file storage, to prevent users from creating setuid files that could pose security risks.
title: 1.1.2.3.3 Ensure nosuid option set on /home partition (Automated)

description: The /var directory is used by daemons and other system services to temporarily store dynamic data. Some directories created by these processes may be world-writable. Mounting /var on a separate partition allows for additional security options and prevents resource exhaustion that could impact the system.
title: 1.1.2.4.1 Ensure separate partition exists for /var (Automated)

description: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices. This ensures that users cannot create a block or character special devices in /var, which is not intended to support devices.
title: 1.1.2.4.2 Ensure nodev option set on /var partition (Automated)

description: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. This is important for the /var filesystem, which is intended for variable files such as logs, to prevent users from creating setuid files in /var.
title: 1.1.2.4.3 Ensure nosuid option set on /var partition (Automated)

description: The /var/tmp directory is a world-writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications. Temporary files residing in /var/tmp are to be preserved between reboots. Configuring /var/tmp as its own file system allows an administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev, limiting an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system.
title: 1.1.2.5.1 Ensure separate partition exists for /var/tmp

description: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices. This ensures that users cannot create a block or character special devices in /var/tmp.
title: 1.1.2.5.2 Ensure nodev option set on /var/tmp partition

description: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. This is important for the /var/tmp filesystem, which is intended for temporary file storage, to prevent users from creating setuid files in this location.
title: 1.1.2.5.3 Ensure nosuid option set on /var/tmp partition

description: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. This is important for the /var/tmp filesystem, which is intended for temporary file storage, to prevent users from running executable binaries from this location.
title: 1.1.2.5.4 Ensure noexec option set on /var/tmp partition

description: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data. Configuring /var/log as its own file system allows an administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev, limiting an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system.
title: 1.1.2.6.1 Ensure separate partition exists for /var/log (Automated)

description: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices. This is important for the /var/log filesystem, which is not intended to support devices, ensuring that users cannot create a block or character special devices in /var/log.
title: 1.1.2.6.2 Ensure nodev option set on /var/log partition

description: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. This is important for the /var/log filesystem, which is intended solely for log files, to prevent users from creating setuid files in this directory.
title: 1.1.2.6.3 Ensure nosuid option set on /var/log partition

description: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries.
title: 1.1.2.6.4 Ensure noexec option set on /var/log partition

description: The auditing daemon, auditd, stores log data in the /var/log/audit directory. Configuring /var/log/audit as its own file system allows an administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system.
title: 1.1.2.7.1 Ensure separate partition exists for /var/log/audit (Automated)

description: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices. This is important for the /var/log/audit filesystem, which is not intended to support devices, ensuring that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/log/audit.
title: 1.1.2.7.2 Ensure nodev option set on /var/log/audit partition

description: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files. This is important for the /var/log/audit filesystem, which is intended for variable files such as logs, to prevent users from creating setuid files in this directory.
title: 1.1.2.7.3 Ensure nosuid option set on /var/log/audit partition

description: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries. This is important for the /var/log/audit filesystem, which is intended solely for audit logs, to prevent users from running executable binaries from this location.
title: 1.1.2.7.4 Ensure noexec option set on /var/log/audit partition

description: Ensure that GPG keys are configured correctly for your system to verify package integrity during and after installation.
title: 1.2.1.1 Ensure GPG keys are configured (Manual)

description: The gpgcheck option controls verifying package signatures after download. This option is configurable as a global option in the main section of /etc/dnf/dnf.conf and a per repository option in individual files in the /etc/yum.repos.d/* directory. The option is enabled if gpgcheck is set to 1, true, or yes. The option is disabled if gpgcheck is set to 0, false, or no. If an invalid option is set, e.g. gpgcheck=2, the global option will be used. Settings in files in the /etc/yum.repos.d/ directory take precedence over the global configuration.
title: 1.2.1.2 Ensure gpgcheck is configured (Automated)

description: Systems need to have the respective package manager repositories configured to ensure that the system is able to receive the latest patches and updates.
title: 1.2.1.4 Ensure package manager repositories are configured

description: The RPM packaging specification allows for 3 levels of dependencies to be declared: hard dependencies (Requires / Provides) for packages which must be installed for a minimal installation of the application to function, weak dependencies (Recommends / Supplements) for packages which provide additional features, but which are not required for a minimal installation to function, and hints (Suggests / Enhances) for packages which offer add-ons which might be useful. Unless a system specifically requires the additional capabilities provided by the weak dependencies, it is recommended that the packages are not installed to reduce the potential attack surface.
title: 1.2.1.5 Ensure weak dependencies are configured (Automated)

description: Security vulnerabilities and functional improvements are regularly addressed through software updates and patches. It is recommended that operating system updates be performed on enterprise assets through automated patch management on a monthly, or more frequent, basis.
title: 1.2.2.1 Ensure updates, patches, and additional security software are installed (Manual)

description: SELinux provides Mandatory Access Control. Without a Mandatory Access Control system installed only the default Discretionary Access Control system will be available.
title: 1.3.1.1 Ensure SELinux is installed (Automated)

description: Configure SELINUX to be enabled at boot time and verify that it has not been overwritten by the grub boot parameters.
title: 1.3.1.2 Ensure SELinux is not disabled in bootloader configuration

description: Configure SELinux to meet or exceed the default targeted policy, which constrains daemons and system software only.
title: 1.3.1.3 Ensure SELinux policy is configured (Automated)

description: Ensure that no unconfined services exist on the system, as they can pose security risks by allowing processes to bypass SELinux protections.
title: 1.3.1.6 Ensure no unconfined services exist (Manual)

description: Setting the boot loader password will require that anyone rebooting the system must enter a password before being able to set command line boot parameters.
title: 1.4.1 Ensure bootloader password is set (Automated)

description: The grub files contain information on boot settings and passwords for unlocking boot options. Setting the permissions to read and write for root only prevents non-root users from seeing the boot parameters or changing them. Non-root users who read the boot parameters may be able to identify weaknesses in security upon boot and be able to exploit them.
title: 1.4.2 Ensure access to bootloader config is configured

description: core - limits the core file size hard - for enforcing hard resource limits. These limits are set by the superuser and enforced by the Kernel. The user cannot raise their requirement of system resources above such values. Setting a hard limit on core dumps prevents users from overriding the soft variable. A core dump includes a memory image taken at the time the operating system terminates an application. The memory image could contain sensitive data and is generally useful only for developers trying to debug problems.
title: 1.5.1 Ensure core file size is configured (Automated)

description: fs.protected_hardlinks Controls the creation of hard links to files. By enabling the fs.protected_hardlinks kernel parameter, users can no longer create soft or hard links to files they do not own. This mitigates vulnerabilities based on unsecure file systems accessed by privileged programs.
title: 1.5.2 Ensure fs.protected_hardlinks is configured (Automated)

description: Verify fs.protected_symlinks is set to 1 in the running configuration and in the systemd sysctl configuration file.
title: 1.5.3 Ensure fs.protected_symlinks is configured (Automated)

description: fs.suid_dumpable governs whether a privileged process (with the setuid bit) can generate a core dump, regardless of other configurations. It is crucial to ensure that this setting is configured to prevent sensitive data from being exposed through core dumps.
title: 1.5.4 Ensure fs.suid_dumpable is configured (Automated)

description: kernel.dmesg_restrict can be used to configure the Linux kernel and prevent unprivileged users access to information from the kernel's log buffer.
title: 1.5.5 Ensure kernel.dmesg_restrict is configured (Automated)

description: Verify that the kernel.kptr_restrict parameter is set to a value of 1 or 2 to ensure kernel addresses are not exposed, enhancing system security.
title: 1.5.6 Ensure kernel.kptr_restrict is configured (Automated)

description: Address space layout randomization (ASLR) is an exploit mitigation technique which randomly arranges the address space of key data areas of a process. This makes it difficult to write memory page exploits as the memory placement will be consistently shifting.
title: 1.5.8 Ensure kernel.randomize_va_space is configured

description: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is generally used to determine why a program aborted. It can also be used to glean confidential information from a core file.
title: 1.5.9 Ensure systemd-coredump ProcessSizeMax is configured

description: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is generally used to determine why a program aborted. It can also be used to glean confidential information from a core file.
regex: systemd-coredump Storage is set to none
title: 1.5.10 Ensure systemd-coredump Storage is configured

description: Ensure that the system-wide crypto policy is not set to LEGACY, which allows outdated and less secure algorithms and protocols, increasing vulnerability to attacks.
title: 1.6.1 Ensure system wide crypto policy is not set to legacy

description: Ensure that the system-wide cryptographic policy disables SHA-1 hash and signature support to mitigate vulnerabilities associated with this weak hash function.
title: 1.6.2 Ensure system wide crypto policy disables sha1 hash and signature support (Automated)

description: Message Authentication Code (MAC) algorithm is a family of cryptographic functions that is parameterized by a symmetric key. Each of the functions can act on input data (called a “message”) of variable length to produce an output value of a specified length. The output value is called the MAC of the input message. A MAC algorithm can be used to provide data-origin authentication and data-integrity protection.
title: 1.6.3 Ensure system wide crypto policy macs are configured

description: Ensure that the system-wide cryptographic policy disables the use of CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode for SSH connections to mitigate vulnerabilities associated with this encryption method.
title: 1.6.4 Ensure system wide crypto policy disables cbc for ssh

description: GDM is the GNOME Display Manager which handles graphical login for GNOME based systems. By using the lockdown mode in dconf, you can prevent users from changing specific settings. Warning messages inform users who are attempting to login to the system of their legal status regarding the system and must include the name of the organization that owns the system and any monitoring policies that are in place.
title: 1.8.1 Ensure GDM login banner is configured (Automated)

description: GNOME Display Manager (GDM) handles graphical login for GNOME based systems. The disable-user-list option controls if a list of users is displayed on the login screen. By using the lockdown mode in dconf, you can prevent users from changing specific settings.
title: 1.8.2 Ensure GDM disable-user-list is configured (Automated)

description: The autorun-never setting allows the GNOME Desktop Display Manager to disable autorun through GDM. This is important to prevent malware from executing when removable media is inserted into a system.
title: 1.8.5 Ensure GDM autorun-never is configured (Automated)

description: Verify that Xwayland is not enabled to mitigate security risks associated with X11 applications running in a Wayland environment.
title: 1.8.6 Ensure Xwayland is configured (Automated)

description: Ensure that the DHCP server services are not in use to reduce the potential attack surface unless the system is specifically set up to act as a DHCP server.
title: 2.1.4 Ensure dhcp server services are not in use (Automated)

description: Ensure that the DNS server services are not in use to reduce the potential attack surface unless the system is designated as a DNS server.
title: 2.1.5 Ensure dns server services are not in use (Automated)

description: Mail Transfer Agents (MTA), such as sendmail and Postfix, are used to listen for incoming mail and transfer the messages to the appropriate user or mail server. If the system is not intended to be a mail server, it is recommended that the MTA be configured to only process local mail.
title: 2.1.21 Ensure mail transfer agents are configured for local-only mode (Automated)

description: Ensure that only approved services are listening on a network interface by reviewing the output of the command and taking necessary actions based on local site policy.
title: 2.1.22 Ensure only approved services are listening on a network interface (Manual)

description: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where no authentication is necessary (permits anonymous users to connect to a server). It is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.
title: 2.2.1 Ensure ftp client is not installed (Automated)

description: Ensure that the openldap-clients package is not installed to reduce the potential attack surface.
title: 2.2.2 Ensure ldap client is not installed (Automated)

description: The telnet package contains the telnet client, which allows users to start connections to other systems via the telnet protocol. The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted, which could allow an unauthorized user to steal credentials. It is advisable to remove the telnet client to prevent accidental or intentional misuse.
title: 2.2.3 Ensure telnet client is not installed (Automated)

description: Ensure that the TFTP client is not installed on the system to prevent potential security vulnerabilities associated with the Trivial File Transfer Protocol.
title: 2.2.4 Ensure tftp client is not installed (Automated)

description: System time should be synchronized between all systems in an environment. This is typically done by establishing an authoritative time server or set of servers and having all systems synchronize their clocks to them.
title: 2.3.1 Ensure time synchronization is in use (Automated)

description: Ensure that the chrony service is configured to use an authorized NTP server for time synchronization, which is critical for maintaining accurate timestamps in logs and supporting security mechanisms.
title: 2.3.2 Ensure chrony is configured (Automated)

description: The cron daemon is used to execute batch jobs on the system. It is essential for running maintenance jobs, including security monitoring tasks.
title: 2.4.1.1 Ensure cron daemon is enabled and active (Automated)

description: The /etc/crontab file is used by cron to control its own jobs. The commands in this item make sure that root is the user and group owner of the file and that only the owner can access the file.
title: 2.4.1.2 Ensure access to /etc/crontab is configured (Automated)

description: This directory contains system cron jobs that need to run on an hourly basis. The files in this directory cannot be manipulated by the crontab command, but are instead edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to user and group root, preventing regular users from accessing this directory.
title: 2.4.1.3 Ensure access to /etc/cron.hourly is configured

description: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains system cron jobs that need to run on a daily basis. The files in this directory cannot be manipulated by the crontab command, but are instead edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to user and group root, preventing regular users from accessing this directory.
title: 2.4.1.4 Ensure access to /etc/cron.daily is configured (Automated)

description: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run on a weekly basis. The files in this directory cannot be manipulated by the crontab command but are instead edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to user and group root, preventing regular users from accessing this directory.
title: 2.4.1.5 Ensure access to /etc/cron.weekly is configured

description: The /etc/cron.monthly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run on a monthly basis. The files in this directory cannot be manipulated by the crontab command but are instead edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to user and group root, preventing regular users from accessing this directory.
title: 2.4.1.6 Ensure access to /etc/cron.monthly is configured

description: The /etc/cron.yearly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run on an annual basis. The files in this directory cannot be manipulated by the crontab command but are instead edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to user and group root, preventing regular users from accessing this directory.
title: 2.4.1.7 Ensure access to /etc/cron.yearly is configured

description: The /etc/cron.d directory contains system cron jobs that need to run in a similar manner to the hourly, daily weekly and monthly jobs from /etc/crontab, but require more granular control as to when they run. The files in this directory cannot be manipulated by the crontab command but are instead edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to user and group root, preventing regular users from accessing this directory.
title: 2.4.1.8 Ensure access to /etc/cron.d is configured (Automated)

description: Configure data access control lists based on a user’s need to know. Apply data access control lists, also known as access permissions, to local and remote file systems, databases, and applications.
title: 3.3 Configure Data Access Control Lists

description: The net.ipv4.ip_forward flag tells the system whether it can forward IPv4 packets or not. Setting net.ipv4.ip_forward to 0 ensures that a system with multiple interfaces will not be able to forward IPv4 packets, which is important for security in non-router configurations.
title: 3.3.1.1 Ensure net.ipv4.ip_forward is configured (Automated)

description: Verify that the net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding parameter is set to 0 to ensure that the system does not forward IPv4 packets, which is unnecessary for non-router configurations.
title: 3.3.1.2 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding is configured

description: Verify that the net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding parameter is set to 0 to ensure that the system does not forward IPv4 packets on newly added network interfaces, which is important for hosts that are not acting as routers.
title: 3.3.1.3 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding is configured

description: ICMP Redirects are used to send routing information to other hosts. As a host itself does not act as a router (in a host only configuration), there is no need to send redirects. net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects controls sending of all IPv4 ICMP redirected packets on all interfaces.
title: 3.3.1.4 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects is configured

description: ICMP Redirects are used to send routing information to other hosts. As a host itself does not act as a router (in a host only configuration), there is no need to send redirects. This control ensures that the system does not send ICMP redirects, which could be exploited by an attacker to corrupt routing information.
title: 3.3.1.5 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects is configured

description: net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses controls if the kernel logs bogus responses (RFC-1122 non-compliant) from broadcast reframes. It is important to ensure this setting is configured to prevent log file system from being filled with useless error messages.
title: 3.3.1.6 Ensure net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses is configured

description: net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts controls if all ICMP echo and timestamp requests to broadcast and multicast addresses are ignored.
title: 3.3.1.7 Ensure net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is configured (Automated)

description: Verify that the system does not accept any IPv4 ICMP redirect messages by checking the configuration of net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects.
title: 3.3.1.8 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured

description: Verify that the net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects is set to 0 to prevent the acceptance of ICMP redirect messages, which can be used to manipulate routing tables.
title: 3.3.1.9 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured

description: Secure ICMP redirects are the same as ICMP redirects, except they come from gateways listed on the default gateway list. It is assumed that these gateways are known to your system, and that they are likely to be secure. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects to 0 will prevent the system from accepting any IPv4 routing table updates by possibly compromised known gateways.
title: 3.3.1.10 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects is configured

description: Secure ICMP redirects are the same as ICMP redirects, except they come from gateways listed on the default gateway list. It is assumed that these gateways are known to your system, and that they are likely to be secure. Setting net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects to 0 will prevent the system from accepting IPv4 routing table updates by possibly compromised known gateways on a newly added network interface.
title: 3.3.1.11 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects is configured

description: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter controls reverse path filtering for IPv4 traffic on all network interfaces. Reverse path filtering is a security mechanism in Linux that helps prevent IP spoofing and other network attacks. When enabled, it checks if the source IP address of an incoming packet is reachable through the same network interface it was received on. If the packet's source address is not reachable through the interface it arrived on, the packet is dropped.
title: 3.3.1.12 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter is configured

description: Verify that the net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route parameter is set to 0.
title: 3.3.1.14 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured (Automated)

description: Verify net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route is set to 0.
title: 3.3.1.15 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured (Automated)

description: When enabled, this feature logs packets with un-routable source addresses to the kernel log. This helps in investigating potential spoofed packets sent by attackers.
title: 3.3.1.16 Ensure net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians is configured

description: Verify net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is set to 1 in the running configuration and in the systemd configuration file.
title: 3.3.1.18 Ensure net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is configured

description: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding flag tells the system whether it can forward IPv6 packets or not. If IPv6 has been disabled, or this system is a router, this recommendation is not applicable. Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding to 0 ensures that a system with multiple interfaces will not be able to forward IPv6 packets.
title: 3.3.2.1 Ensure net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding is configured

description: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding flag tells the system whether it can forward IPv6 on the default or newly added network interface. If IPv6 is enabled, it should be set to 0 to prevent unnecessary network information transmission.
title: 3.3.2.2 Ensure net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding is configured

description: Verify that the net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects is set to 0, ensuring that the system does not accept any IPv6 ICMP redirect messages, which could allow outsiders to update the system's routing tables.
title: 3.3.2.3 Ensure net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured

description: Verify that the net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects is set to 0, ensuring that the system does not accept IPv6 ICMP redirect messages on a newly added network interface.
title: 3.3.2.4 Ensure net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured (Automated)

description: Verify that the net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra is set to 0 to ensure that the system does not accept router advertisements, which could lead to routing traffic to compromised machines.
title: 3.3.2.7 Ensure net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra is configured

description: Verify that the net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra is set to 0 to ensure that the system does not accept router advertisements, which could lead to routing traffic to compromised machines.
title: 3.3.2.8 Ensure net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra is configured

description: Ensure that the firewalld package is installed on the system to manage firewall rules effectively.
title: 4.1.1 Ensure firewalld is installed (Automated)

description: The FirewallBackend option selects the firewall backend implementation. Verifying the proper backend configuration ensures the critical functionality of the firewall.
title: 4.1.2 Ensure firewalld backend is configured (Automated)

description: Implement and manage a firewall on servers, where supported. Example implementations include a virtual firewall, operating system firewall, or a third-party firewall agent.
title: 4.4 Implement and Manage a Firewall on Servers

description: Implement and manage a host-based firewall or port-filtering tool on end-user devices, with a default-deny rule that drops all traffic except those services and ports that are explicitly allowed.
title: 4.5 Implement and Manage a Firewall on End-User Devices

description: The file /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and files ending in .conf in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d directory, contain configuration specifications for sshd. These specifications need to be protected from unauthorized changes by non-privileged users.
title: 5.1.1 Ensure access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured

description: Ensure that SSH private host key files are owned by the root user and have appropriate group ownership and permissions to prevent unauthorized access.
title: 5.1.2 Ensure access to SSH private host key files is configured

description: Ensure access to SSH public host key files is configured. This control verifies that SSH public host key files have the correct permissions and ownership to prevent unauthorized access, which could compromise the SSH service.
title: 5.1.3 Ensure access to SSH public host key files is configured

description: The GSSAPIAuthentication parameter specifies whether user authentication based on GSSAPI is allowed. It should be disabled to reduce the attack surface of the system.
title: 5.1.9 Ensure sshd GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled (Automated)

description: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies if authentication is allowed through trusted hosts via the user of .rhosts, or /etc/hosts.equiv, along with successful public key client host authentication.
title: 5.1.10 Ensure sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled

description: Use unique passwords for all enterprise assets. Best practice implementation includes, at a minimum, an 8-character password for accounts using MFA and a 14-character password for accounts not using MFA.
title: 5.2 Use Unique Passwords

description: Ensure that local logging has been enabled on all systems and networking devices.
title: 6.2 Activate audit logging

description: Enable system logging to include detailed information such as an event source, date, user, timestamp, source addresses, destination addresses, and other useful elements.
title: 6.3 Enable Detailed Logging

description: auditd is the userspace component to the Linux Auditing System. It's responsible for writing audit records to the disk. The capturing of system events provides system administrators with information to allow them to determine if unauthorized access to their system is occurring.
title: 6.3.1.1 Ensure auditd packages are installed (Automated)

description: Configure grub2 so that processes that are capable of being audited can be audited even if they start up prior to auditd startup.
title: 6.3.1.2 Ensure auditing for processes that start prior to auditd is enabled (Automated)

description: The audit_backlog_limit parameter determines how auditd records can be held in the auditd backlog. The default setting of 64 may be insufficient to store all audit events during boot.
title: 6.3.1.3 Ensure audit_backlog_limit is configured (Automated)

description: Turn on the auditd daemon to record system events.
title: 6.3.1.4 Ensure auditd service is enabled and active (Automated)

description: Configure the maximum size of the audit log file. Once the log reaches the maximum size, it will be rotated and a new log file will be started.
title: 6.3.2.1 Ensure audit log storage size is configured (Automated)

description: Ensure that actions performed as another user are always logged to maintain an audit trail of users with temporary elevated privileges.
title: 6.3.3.2 Ensure actions as another user are always logged

description: Record changes to network environment files or system calls related to hostname and domain name modifications. This ensures that any unauthorized changes to the host and domain names are detected, which could affect security parameters.
title: 6.3.3.5 Ensure events that modify sethostname and setdomainname are collected (Automated)

description: Record changes to network environment files or system calls. The files being monitored are: /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net - messages displayed pre-login. Monitoring /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net is important, as intruders could put disinformation into those files and trick users into providing information to the intruder.
title: 6.3.3.6 Ensure events that modify /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net are collected (Automated)

description: Record changes to network environment files or system calls. The files being monitored are: /etc/hosts and /etc/hostname. This ensures that unauthorized modifications are detected, which could indicate an intruder attempting to manipulate machine associations.
title: 6.3.3.7 Ensure events that modify /etc/hosts and /etc/hostname are collected (Automated)

description: Record changes to network environment files or system calls. The files being monitored are: /etc/NetworkManager/ - directory contains configuration files and settings used by the NetworkManager. Monitoring the /etc/NetworkManager/ directory will identify potential unauthorized changes to network configuration files.
title: 6.3.3.9 Ensure events that modify /etc/NetworkManager directory are collected (Automated)

description: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful uses of the setfacl command.
title: 6.3.3.28 Ensure successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are collected (Automated)

description: Set -c flag so that auditctl will continue loading rules in spite of an error. The exit code will not be success if any rule fails to load.
title: 6.3.3.35 Ensure the audit configuration is loaded regardless of errors (Automated)

description: Set system audit so that audit rules cannot be modified with auditctl. Setting the flag "-e 2" forces audit to be put in immutable mode. Audit changes can only be made on system reboot.
title: 6.3.3.36 Ensure the audit configuration is immutable (Automated)

description: Ensure that the running and on disk configuration of the audit system is the same to avoid discrepancies that could lead to compliance issues.
title: 6.3.3.37 Ensure the running and on disk configuration is the same

description: Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity. Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising its confidentiality.
title: 6.3.4.4 Ensure audit log files group owner is configured

description: Audit configuration files control auditd and what events are audited. Access to the audit configuration files could allow unauthorized personnel to prevent the auditing of critical events. Misconfigured audit configuration files may prevent the auditing of critical events or impact the system's performance by overwhelming the audit log. Misconfiguration of the audit configuration files may also make it more difficult to establish and investigate events relating to an incident.
title: 6.3.4.6 Ensure audit configuration files owner is configured

description: Audit configuration files control auditd and what events are audited. Access to the audit configuration files could allow unauthorized personnel to prevent the auditing of critical events. Misconfigured audit configuration files may prevent the auditing of critical events or impact the system's performance by overwhelming the audit log. Misconfiguration of the audit configuration files may also make it more difficult to establish and investigate events relating to an incident.
title: 6.3.4.7 Ensure audit configuration files group owner is configured

description: Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open source audit tools needed to successfully view and manipulate audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.
title: 6.3.4.10 Ensure audit tools group owner is configured

description: The /etc/passwd file contains user account information that is used by many system utilities and therefore must be readable for these utilities to operate. It is critical to ensure that the /etc/passwd file is protected from unauthorized write access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
title: 7.1.1 Ensure access to /etc/passwd is configured (Automated)

description: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information. It is critical to ensure that the /etc/passwd- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
title: 7.1.2 Ensure access to /etc/passwd- is configured (Automated)

description: The /etc/group file contains a list of all the valid groups defined in the system. The command below allows read/write access for root and read access for everyone else. The /etc/group file needs to be protected from unauthorized changes by non-privileged users, but needs to be readable as this information is used with many non-privileged programs.
title: 7.1.3 Ensure access to /etc/group is configured (Automated)

description: The /etc/group- file contains a backup list of all the valid groups defined in the system. It is critical to ensure that the /etc/group- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
title: 7.1.4 Ensure access to /etc/group- is configured (Automated)

description: The /etc/shadow file is used to store the information about user accounts that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
title: 7.1.5 Ensure access to /etc/shadow is configured (Automated)

description: The /etc/shadow- file is used to store backup information about user accounts that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
title: 7.1.6 Ensure access to /etc/shadow- is configured (Automated)

description: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store the information about groups that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information. Ensuring proper access configuration is vital to prevent unauthorized access and potential exploitation.
title: 7.1.7 Ensure access to /etc/gshadow is configured (Automated)

description: The /etc/gshadow- file is used to store backup information about groups that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information. It is essential to ensure that the /etc/gshadow- file is protected from unauthorized access, as its permissions could be altered either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
title: 7.1.8 Ensure access to /etc/gshadow- is configured (Automated)

description: /etc/shells is a text file which contains the full pathnames of valid login shells. This file is consulted by chsh and available to be queried by other programs. It is critical to ensure that the /etc/shells file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.
title: 7.1.9 Ensure access to /etc/shells is configured (Automated)

description: Ensure that the access permissions for /etc/security/opasswd and its backup /etc/security/opasswd.old are set to 600 or more restrictive, with ownership by root (Uid 0 and Gid 0). This is critical to protect previous user passwords from unauthorized access.
title: 7.1.10 Ensure access to /etc/security/opasswd is configured

description: World writable files are the least secure. Data in world-writable files can be modified and compromised by any user on the system. World writable files may also indicate an incorrectly written script or program that could potentially be the cause of a larger compromise to the system's integrity. Setting the sticky bit on world writable directories prevents users from deleting or renaming files in that directory that are not owned by them.
title: 7.1.11 Ensure world writable files and directories are secured

description: The owner of a file can set the file's permissions to run with the owner's or group's permissions, even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group. It is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate.
title: 7.1.13 Ensure SUID and SGID files are reviewed (Manual)

description: Local accounts can use shadowed passwords. With shadowed passwords, the passwords are saved in shadow password file, /etc/shadow, encrypted by a salted one-way hash. Accounts with a shadowed password have an x in the second field in /etc/passwd.
title: 7.2.1 Ensure accounts in /etc/passwd use shadowed passwords

description: An account with an empty password field means that anybody may log in as that user without providing a password.
title: 7.2.2 Ensure /etc/shadow password fields are not empty

description: Ensure all groups defined in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group to maintain proper group permissions and enhance system security.
title: 7.2.3 Ensure all groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group

description: Ensure that no duplicate User IDs (UIDs) exist in the system to maintain accountability and appropriate access protections.
title: 7.2.4 Ensure no duplicate UIDs exist (Automated)

description: Ensure that no duplicate Group IDs (GIDs) exist in the system to maintain accountability and appropriate access protections.
title: 7.2.5 Ensure no duplicate GIDs exist (Automated)

description: Ensure that no duplicate user names exist in the system, as this can lead to security issues where multiple users share the same UID, causing access control problems.
title: 7.2.6 Ensure no duplicate user names exist (Automated)

description: Ensure that no duplicate group names exist in the system, as this can lead to security issues with shared GIDs.
title: 7.2.7 Ensure no duplicate group names exist (Automated)

description: Ensure local interactive user home directories are configured to prevent unauthorized access and ensure proper ownership and permissions.
title: 7.2.8 Ensure local interactive user home directories are configured (Automated)

description: Ensure that local interactive user dot files are configured with secure permissions to prevent unauthorized access and modifications by malicious users.
title: 7.2.9 Ensure local interactive user dot files access is configured
